# Untethered

The thing about having a blank page is that it promises freedom and delivers vertigo instead. I'm supposed to write whatever comes to me, which sounds simple until you realize that *everything* comes to you. All of it, simultaneously. The weight of all possible words, all possible directions, all the voices that have ever written anything meaningful suddenly crowding your consciousness like passengers on an overbooked train.

I think about how we're always told to write what we know, but nobody tells you that what you know is surprisingly limited when you actually sit down to examine it. I know, for instance, that it's currently raining outside my window. Not a dramatic rain—the kind that accumulates in droplets before sliding down in rivulets, leaving temporary paths like tiny rivers finding their way down glass. I know the sound it makes when it hits the gutter, a hollow percussion that's almost musical if you're in the right headspace. I know that in about twenty minutes, I'll probably make tea, and I'll use the same mug I've used for three days straight without washing it because I live alone and nobody is here to judge me.

But does any of this matter? Does anyone care about my tea mug?

I think about the people who will read this, if anyone reads this. I imagine them scrolling through on their phones, half-present, waiting for something to grab them. Something clever. Something that makes them feel less alone, or more understood, or—at the very least—entertained enough to keep scrolling instead of switching to another tab. The pressure of being interesting to strangers is extraordinary when you think about it. We've built a world where everyone is constantly performing for an invisible audience, curating their lives into digestible content. And here I am, doing the same thing, pretending this is some kind of genuine outpouring while I'm simultaneously aware of you, reading it, judging whether it's worth your time.

The rain is getting heavier now. It sounds different—more urgent. More honest, somehow.

I've been thinking about time a lot lately. How it doesn't actually feel like the linear thing they taught us about in school. Minutes expand and contract depending on what you're doing. Waiting for something is different from remembering something, which is different from anticipating something. When I was a child, summer lasted forever. Now a season evaporates between coffee cups. I've read that this is because each year is a smaller percentage of your total life as you age, so it *feels* faster. Mathematics explaining the human experience. There's something both comforting and terrifying about that.

I wonder if I'm the only person who sometimes forgets how old I am for a second, and then has to mentally calculate it. I wonder if everyone does this, or if I'm just bad with numbers and self-awareness.

There's a philosophy question I read once: if you replace every plank on a ship, is it still the same ship? I think about my body the same way. Every seven years or so, most of our cells are replaced. So am I the same person I was seven years ago? Ten? The me from childhood seems like a completely different entity—different beliefs, different fears, different versions of what happiness looks like. The continuity is just consciousness, I think. Just the thread of awareness running through all these different bodies, all these different versions.

It's not very comforting, when you think about it.

But then again, maybe that's okay. Maybe we're not supposed to stay the same. Maybe the whole point is to be permeable—to let experiences and time and other people's kindness and cruelty wash through us, changing our shape. I've noticed that the people I know who seem most at peace are the ones who stopped trying to be consistent versions of themselves. They're just... trying. Just being. Adjusting.

I'm not very good at that yet.

The rain is stopping now. I can tell because the sound has changed again—becomes more sporadic, less confident in its purpose. Soon there will be patches of blue, and the light will come back strange and golden through the clouds. Everything will look washed clean and temporary, like it's all been given a second chance.

I used to think I needed to have everything figured out before I could write about it. That I needed resolution and answers and a point. But maybe that's not how it works. Maybe the point is just in the noticing. In sitting with a cup of tea and a window and a random assortment of thoughts, and letting them exist without tying them up into something neat and concluding.

Tomorrow, the rain will be forgotten. I'll walk around outside and step over puddles and think about something else entirely. I'll probably make tea in that same mug, and at some point I'll actually wash it. Life will continue its small accumulations—moments, conversations, quiet failures, tiny unexpected joys—and I'll either be present for them or I won't, and either way, time will keep doing its strange elastic thing.

The blank page isn't actually blank, I think now. It's full of everything. It's full of rain sounds and tea mugs and the weight of all the words that have ever mattered to anyone. It's full of time that can't be held and people who are different every seven years and the quiet terror of trying to say something true.

What comes to me, when I stop trying so hard to be interesting, is just this: I'm here. We're here. The rain falls on the window, and we're underneath a roof, reading words that someone typed into the void hoping they would matter.

And maybe they do. Not because they're clever or perfect or complete, but because they're honest. Because they're real. Because someone bothered to sit down and try.

That seems like enough.
